problem: The answer is wrong for the machine in the chapter. In the ε-free NFA of step 9, δ'(q0,a) = {q0,q1} and δ'({q0,q1},b) = {q2,q3}, so reading ab ends in the set {q2,q3}, which contains q3. With F = {q3}, ab is still accepted. In fact every set produced after a move is already ε-closed (q2 never appears without q3), so for this machine F = {q3} and F' = {q2,q3} accept exactly the same strings — no string is wrongly rejected. The stated reason ('q2 had a free move to q3') describes deleting edges by hand, not the construction the chapter teaches.
fix: Reword the question to the by-hand deletion case: 'A student deletes the two ε-edges from the figure's machine, keeps every symbol edge, and keeps F = {q3}. Which strings are now wrongly rejected, and what is the fix?' Answer: 'b and ab are wrongly rejected, because q0 can no longer slide to q1 before reading b, and q2 can no longer slide to q3. The fix is not only to change the finals: use δ'(q,a) = ECLOSE(δ(ECLOSE(q),a)) for every state and symbol, and set F' = {q | ECLOSE(q) ∩ F ≠ ∅}.'

problem: lex and flex do not run an ε-NFA by tracking state sets with closures. They build a Thompson NFA, then convert it to a DFA by subset construction, and the generated scanner runs that DFA. The claim that they avoid building a full DFA is false for these two tools.
fix: Say instead: 'lex and flex turn regular expressions into ε-NFAs and then into a DFA by subset construction, and the generated scanner runs the DFA. Some newer libraries fall back to simulating the ε-NFA with state sets and closures when the DFA would grow too large, which saves memory on big rule sets.'

problem: The formula writes 2<sup>Q</sup> but the explanation just after it writes '2Q is the set of all subsets of Q'. Without the superscript it reads like an ordinary product.
fix: Write '2<sup>Q</sup> (the power set of Q) is the set of all subsets of Q'.

problem: 'Closing before the move gives a different, wrong set' is misleading. The set you move from must already be closed — that is exactly why the run starts at ECLOSE(q0) — and closing a closed set changes nothing. What actually goes wrong is dropping the closure after the move.
fix: Say: 'Dropping the closure after the move. The set produced by the symbol move is not closed, so always take ECLOSE of it. And move only from a closed set, which is why the run starts at ECLOSE(q0).'
